stem: A fleet of delivery vans publishes JSON telemetry to a Pub/Sub topic. The analytics team needs every message stored in a BigQuery table within seconds. No filtering, enrichment or aggregation is needed, and the team wants the fewest components to monitor and the lowest cost. Which design fits?

choices.text: Create a push subscription that calls a Cloud Run service, which inserts each message into the table
Run a Dataproc cluster with Spark Structured Streaming that reads the topic and appends rows to the table
Run a streaming Dataflow job that reads a pull subscription and writes each message to the table
Create a BigQuery subscription on the topic so Pub/Sub writes the messages to the table directly

stem: A payments company processes several gigabytes of Pub/Sub messages per second with a fleet of worker processes running in a private VPC network. The environment cannot expose a public HTTPS endpoint with a non-self-signed certificate. Throughput and efficient batching matter more than anything else. Which subscription type should the team choose?

choices.text: A push subscription behind an internal load balancer, because messages are delivered one per request
A push subscription, because Pub/Sub then controls flow and no client library is needed
A pull subscription, because workers request batches and the client controls the delivery rate
A BigQuery subscription, because it removes the need for any consumer to process the messages

stem: Four product teams publish order events to a shared Pub/Sub topic. Subscribers keep breaking because some publishers send events with missing or misnamed fields. The data engineering lead wants the field names and types defined centrally and malformed events rejected at publish time. What should be done?

choices.text: Attach a Pub/Sub schema in Avro or Protocol Buffer format to the topic so non-conforming messages are not published
Give each publishing team a separate topic and let each team document its own field names and types independently
Add a Dataflow step in every subscriber pipeline that drops events with unexpected fields after they are delivered
Turn on message ordering on the subscription so that malformed events are delivered after valid events

stem: Which TWO of the following workloads are good candidates for Dataflow at-least-once streaming mode, accepting occasional duplicates in return for lower cost and latency? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A job that appends the current processing time to each message, where the timestamp is stored as the record key
A map-only job that parses application logs and writes them to BigQuery, where a downstream view removes duplicates
A job that keeps a running per-card transaction count used by a fraud-detection rule
A job that sums order quantities per product to drive an ecommerce inventory dashboard
An ETL job that only translates each change record to a target schema, with no aggregation

stem: A data engineer with the project Owner role launches a Dataflow Flex template that reads a Pub/Sub subscription and writes to a BigQuery dataset in another project. Workers start, but the job fails with permission errors on the destination dataset. The engineer's own account can write to that dataset. What should be fixed?

choices.text: Recreate the template specification file in Cloud Storage so the job inherits the engineer's permissions
Grant the engineer's user account a Dataflow Admin role on the destination project
Grant the destination dataset access to the worker service account that the job's VMs run as
Grant the Owner role to the Dataflow service agent used by the service to create worker VMs

stem: A streaming Dataflow job reads from Pub/Sub and serves a latency-sensitive application. The business accepts losing a few seconds of data during a rare regional outage, but wants processing to resume in another region quickly and does not want to pay for a full duplicate pipeline running at all times. Which design matches?

choices.text: Rely on the Dataflow service to move the failed job automatically to another region without any prior configuration
Wait for the region to recover and restart the job from the same subscription, because messages are kept
Run identical pipelines in two regions all the time, both writing to the same sink without any coordination of their outputs, so one region can take over
Keep two independent subscriptions on the topic, one per region, and start a replacement job on the backup subscription

stem: A new version of a subscriber application was deployed and, because of a bug, acknowledged thousands of Pub/Sub messages without processing them. The fix is ready. The team wants to reprocess the messages published during the faulty deployment window. What should they have in place to make this possible?

choices.text: A dead-letter topic on the subscription, because acknowledged messages are automatically forwarded to it for later review
Message retention on the topic or on acknowledged messages, then seek to a time before the deployment
A push endpoint on the subscription, because push subscriptions can redeliver messages that were acknowledged earlier
Exactly-once delivery on the subscription, because it keeps every acknowledged message available for redelivery whenever the subscriber client asks for a new copy

stem: A Dataflow streaming job reads clickstream events from Pub/Sub and builds per-customer session windows. An engineer proposes enabling message ordering with ordering keys on the subscription so events arrive in order. What is the best guidance?

choices.text: Leave ordering disabled on the subscription; Dataflow handles order through event-time windowing, and ordering keys can slow the pipeline
Enable ordering and publish with the same key from every region, so that one global order holds
Enable ordering only on the dead-letter topic, because Dataflow reads dead-letter messages in publication order
Enable ordering with the customer ID as key, because Dataflow requires an ordered subscription to build session windows

stem: A streaming pipeline must output, every minute, the average temperature over the most recent five minutes for each sensor group. Consecutive results should overlap. Which windowing choice produces this?

choices.text: Hopping (sliding) windows five minutes long that start every minute
A global window with a trigger that fires after every minute of processing time
Session windows with a five-minute gap duration per sensor group
Tumbling (fixed) windows five minutes long with no overlap

stem: A news site wants a streaming job that reports page views per hour of the day, one report for each clock hour, with every event counted in exactly one report. Which windowing choice fits?

choices.text: Hopping (sliding) windows of one hour that start every ten minutes
Tumbling (fixed) windows of one hour, applied to the event timestamps
Session windows with a one-hour gap duration for each page
Hopping windows of two hours that start every hour

stem: A mobile game wants to compute, for every player, the total time spent in each play session. A session ends when the player has produced no events for ten minutes, and sessions differ greatly in length. Which windowing function fits?

choices.text: Tumbling windows of ten minutes applied across all players
Tumbling windows of one hour, with a trigger firing on every element
Session windows with a ten-minute gap duration, keyed by player
Hopping windows of ten minutes with a one-minute period

stem: A pipeline counts web orders in hourly windows by event time. Mobile clients buffer events while offline, so some orders arrive up to 30 minutes after the hour has ended. With default settings the hourly counts are too low. Which change gives the most accurate results while still producing timely preliminary numbers?

choices.text: Switch the windows from event time to processing time so every order is counted in the hour in which the pipeline received it, however late the client sent it
Replace the hourly tumbling windows with a global window and a single end-of-stream trigger
Disable the watermark so no element is ever considered late and every window waits for all data
Allow late data (allowed lateness) and add a trigger that emits updated results when late elements arrive

stem: Which TWO statements about watermarks and triggers in a Dataflow streaming pipeline are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: By default a window emits its aggregated result when the watermark passes the end of that window
The pipeline author sets the watermark as a fixed delay behind the wall clock in the Apache Beam SDK
A trigger can only be defined on processing time, because event time is unknown to the runner until a window closes
An element whose timestamp lies in a window that the watermark has already passed is always processed normally
The data source determines the watermark, which signals when the pipeline expects all data for a window to have arrived

stem: A streaming pipeline counts clicks per five-minute window. After a six-hour network outage at the collectors, the backlog was delivered all at once. The dashboard now shows a huge spike in the five minutes after recovery and nothing for the outage window. Which fix addresses the cause?

choices.text: Replace the five-minute tumbling windows with session windows so the backlog forms one large session
Increase the maximum number of workers so the backlog is processed faster and the spike is shorter
Switch the sink from BigQuery to Bigtable so the spike is written with a lower write latency
Take the window timestamp from the click event's own time field instead of the arrival time at the pipeline

stem: A production streaming Dataflow job runs on worker VMs that run the whole pipeline and use large Persistent Disks. Scaling is slow after traffic jumps, and worker CPU and memory are heavily used. The team wants shuffle and state moved off the workers and finer-grained autoscaling. The job must not lose buffered data. What is the right approach?

choices.text: Update the running job in place with the Streaming Engine option enabled
Drain the job, then launch it again with Streaming Engine enabled
Cancel the job immediately and relaunch it with larger worker machine types
Keep the job but add more Persistent Disk to every worker VM

stem: A streaming job that does not use Streaming Engine was launched with a maximum of 20 workers. Ahead of a campaign, an engineer updates the job and sets a maximum of 60 workers, expecting more capacity, but the job cannot scale beyond its original size. What explains this and what is the remedy?

choices.text: The job needs a larger worker machine type, because the worker count is capped by vCPU quota rather than by job options
The update succeeded, but Dataflow applies a new worker maximum only after midnight UTC, so the job must simply wait
Without Streaming Engine the job is bound to the workers and disks allocated at launch, so relaunch with a higher maximum
Horizontal Autoscaling is not supported for streaming jobs, so the count can never exceed Pub/Sub partitions

stem: A Streaming Engine job processes non-urgent audit events. The business accepts a few minutes of extra delay if that reduces worker cost. Which autoscaling setting expresses this preference?

choices.text: Set the autoscaling algorithm to NONE and fix the worker count to the peak value
Configure a higher latency tier so the autoscaler waits for more backlog before it adds workers
Raise the minimum number of workers so that the pipeline always has spare capacity
Switch to a lower latency tier so that the autoscaler reacts to even the smallest backlog by adding workers quickly

stem: A streaming Dataflow job writes enriched events to Bigtable. Autoscaling raises the worker count when the Pub/Sub backlog grows, but the backlog keeps growing, output throughput stays flat and Bigtable cluster CPU is saturated. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Enable exactly-once streaming mode, because duplicate writes are what saturates the nodes
Move the Pub/Sub subscription to a push configuration to reduce the load on Bigtable
Add nodes to the Bigtable cluster, since write parallelism is determined by the number of cluster nodes
Increase the maximum number of Dataflow workers further, because the sink scales with the worker count

stem: A team must replace a running streaming pipeline with a new version in which two transforms were renamed. They want to keep the job's state and buffered data, and avoid launching a replacement that fails its compatibility check. Which TWO actions should they take? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Supply a transform name mapping that links each renamed transform to its old name
Turn off Horizontal Autoscaling on the running job, as the compatibility check requires a fixed worker count
Set the update compatibility version to the SDK version of the new pipeline code
Cancel the running job, so that its buffered data is dropped before the replacement starts
Validate the replacement job graph first by using the graph validate only service option

stem: A streaming job is draining before a planned release but never finishes. The log shows the same exception repeating in a DoFn that parses a field the producers changed. The team does not want to lose buffered data. What should they do?

choices.text: Wait indefinitely, since Dataflow skips records that repeatedly fail and the drain finishes by itself
Start a second identical job on the same subscription so that it takes over the failing records
Cancel the draining job at once and restart from the earliest unread message, accepting the lost buffered data
Update the draining job with code that fixes the parsing error so that the drain can complete

stem: Which TWO statements about the BigQuery write methods of the Dataflow BigQuery connector in streaming pipelines are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The STORAGE_API_AT_LEAST_ONCE mode guarantees that no duplicate rows are ever written
The legacy streaming inserts mode is the default for unbounded collections, but it uses best-effort deduplication and is not recommended for new projects
Streaming inserts provide exactly-once semantics and cost less than the Storage Write API
The FILE_LOADS method is the recommended choice when the pipeline runs in at-least-once streaming mode
The Storage Write API mode (STORAGE_WRITE_API) provides exactly-once semantics

stem: A streaming pipeline writes parsed events to BigQuery with the Storage Write API. A producer sometimes sends rows whose values do not fit the table schema. These rows must not block the pipeline, and the team wants to inspect and reprocess them later. What design fits?

choices.text: Remove the schema from the destination table so that every row is accepted regardless of its fields
Let the pipeline fail on the first bad row, so the Dataflow retries stop the data from entering BigQuery
Drop failed rows silently in the connector, because streaming pipelines cannot keep a record of them
Collect failed rows as a separate PCollection and write them to a dead-letter table or bucket

stem: A subscriber on a Pub/Sub pull subscription repeatedly fails on one malformed message. Each retry blocks capacity and the same message keeps coming back. The team wants such messages moved aside after a limited number of attempts. What should they configure?

choices.text: A dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempts value, plus publish and subscribe roles for the Pub/Sub service account
A Cloud Storage subscription on the topic, which automatically excludes messages that a subscriber cannot parse
Message ordering on the subscription, so that the malformed message is skipped because it has an empty ordering key and is treated as unordered
A shorter message retention duration on the topic, so the malformed message is deleted before it is redelivered

stem: A team wants one reusable Dataflow template whose pipeline selects a different I/O connector depending on a parameter and validates the input parameters before the job starts. Which template type fits, and why?

choices.text: A classic template, because values wrapped in ValueProvider can alter which connector the static graph uses
A classic template, because its job graph is a JSON serialization that can be changed by parameters at launch
A Flex template, because the graph is built at launch from runtime parameters and can be validated first
A Flex template, because it avoids Docker images and keeps the whole pipeline definition only in a Cloud Storage file

stem: A platform team wants analysts to start a vetted streaming pipeline with their own parameters, without installing the Apache Beam SDK. The pipeline code must live in source control and ship through CI/CD. What should the platform team create?

choices.text: A Pub/Sub topic whose subscribers compile and run the pipeline when a message with parameters arrives
A Dataflow template stored as a versioned artifact that analysts launch with parameters
A shared VM image that has the Beam SDK installed, from which each analyst runs the pipeline code
A Dataproc workflow template that analysts instantiate to run the Beam pipeline on a cluster

stem: Which TWO statements about Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: With the feature on, subscribers no longer have to acknowledge within the acknowledgment deadline
Exactly-once delivery guarantees a single delivery across every region where subscribers connect worldwide
Only pull subscriptions, including subscribers that use StreamingPull, support exactly-once delivery
Push subscriptions support exactly-once delivery if the endpoint answers each request quickly
Exactly-once delivery is provided within a cloud region and is based on a unique message ID defined by Pub/Sub

stem: A Streaming Engine job aggregates events per customer ID in windows that stay open for a long time. One placeholder customer ID, used for all anonymous visitors, receives a very large share of events. The job becomes stuck with rising system lag and a log message saying a limit on aggregated data per key was exceeded. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Redesign the key so anonymous traffic is spread across many keys by adding a shard component, then combine partial results
Disable Streaming Engine so that state is held on worker disks, which have no per-key limit
Raise the worker machine type to a high-memory shape, because the limit applies to each worker's memory and not to the key
Convert the windows to a global window so the state for the key is released after every element

stem: An engineer reads new CSV files that land in a Cloud Storage bucket, using a file-based source and the streaming flag, expecting a continuously running job. The job processes the files present at start and then stops. What is the design change that gives continuous processing?

choices.text: Switch to a Flex template, because only template-launched streaming jobs can remain running once their source has ended
Increase the minimum number of workers so that the job has no idle capacity at which to shut down
Enable at-least-once streaming mode, which keeps a job alive when its bounded source is exhausted
Have the bucket send notifications to Pub/Sub and read the subscription from the streaming pipeline

stem: A compliance team stores 150,000 contract-clause embeddings in a BigQuery table and runs a few similarity searches per day. Reviewers must always see the true closest clauses, because a missed clause is a legal risk, and the latency of each search is not important. How should the data engineer run the searches?

choices.text: Export the embeddings to a spreadsheet and ask reviewers to sort the clauses by similarity score manually
Run VECTOR_SEARCH without a vector index, or force brute force, so every stored vector is compared and results are exact
Create a vector index and rely on approximate nearest neighbor results, since index-backed search always returns the same clauses as an exhaustive scan
Replace the stored embeddings with lower-dimension vectors so approximate search becomes exact on the smaller table

stem: A retailer generated product embeddings in BigQuery with a text embedding model that Google has announced will be retired. The team moves the pipeline to the replacement model. Which TWO actions keep similarity search results meaningful? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Apply L2 normalization to the old vectors so they share an embedding space with the replacement model's vectors
Keep the stored vectors and embed only new rows with the replacement model, because the vector length is unchanged
Keep embedding search queries with the retiring model until its retirement date, then switch only the table
Regenerate the embeddings already stored in the table with the replacement model, then rebuild any vector index on that column
Generate each search query's embedding with the same replacement model that produced the stored table embeddings

stem: An insurer wants an assistant that answers questions from 20,000 long policy PDFs. A data engineer is preparing the corpus in BigQuery for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Which preparation step is most important before generating embeddings?

choices.text: Split extracted text into passage-sized chunks, one row per chunk with a document identifier and metadata, then embed each chunk
Concatenate all PDFs into one very long text row per product line so each embedding carries the whole context
Convert the PDF text into one-hot encoded word columns, which can then be searched with vector search directly
Embed only the title of each PDF, because titles are short and always describe the full document content accurately, then pass whole PDFs to the model

stem: A media company has precomputed embeddings for 8 million catalog items. Every night a job must find the 20 most similar items for each of 400,000 newly added items, and finish within the batch window. Which BigQuery capability fits best?

choices.text: A scheduled query that exports all embeddings to Cloud Storage so a spreadsheet macro can rank neighbors
AI.SIMILARITY called in a cross join between new and catalog items, computing a cosine similarity for every pair
VECTOR_SEARCH over the embeddings, with a vector index on the catalog table to speed up the nearest neighbor lookups
A LIKE predicate on item titles, ordered by the number of shared words, to approximate semantic similarity

stem: A team plans to add semantic search over 500 million embeddings in BigQuery and wants to forecast cost. Which TWO statements about the cost of vector search are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Index building is billed per row indexed at a fixed rate, whatever the total size of the indexed data
A vector index adds no storage cost, because index data is kept in a hidden system area
Active vector indexes incur storage costs, and the index size is visible in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VECTOR_INDEXES
Vector search queries are accelerated by BI Engine, which removes the slot or scan charge for repeated searches
With on-demand pricing, a vector search is charged for bytes scanned in the base table, the index and the search query

stem: A bank holds 60 million customer records from three systems, with names and addresses typed differently in each. Exact joins miss many duplicates. The data engineer wants to prepare a deduplication step in BigQuery with the least custom infrastructure. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Export records to a self-managed server that runs a fuzzy matching service, then load the match results back into BigQuery
Delete every record that shares a postal code with another record, since records that live close together are duplicates
Hash every record with a cryptographic hash and join on equal hashes, since identical meaning always gives identical hashes for names and addresses typed in several formats
Embed a normalized text form of each record, use vector search for nearest-neighbor candidates, and review matches above a threshold

stem: A vector search runs against a 4 TB table of embeddings that holds ten years of support tickets, and analysts always want only the last 30 days. Queries scan far more data than expected, even with the vector index in place. The table is partitioned by ticket date. Which change reduces the scanned data most directly?

choices.text: Pre-filter on the partitioned date column in the VECTOR_SEARCH call so only recent partitions are read
Cluster the table on an unrelated column and filter on it in a subquery without storing that column in the vector index
Switch the embedding column to a string type so that BigQuery can prune data with its text search index
Drop the vector index so that the function compares only the vectors returned by a later WHERE clause

stem: A weather-data company wants to give about 40 customer companies, each with its own Google Cloud organization, read access to a curated, continuously updated BigQuery dataset. The company does not want to copy the data per customer, and each customer should pay for its own queries. What should the data engineer use?

choices.text: Add each customer's users to the dataset with the BigQuery Admin role on the publisher's project so they can query directly
Publish a listing in an Analytics Hub (BigQuery sharing) data exchange so each customer subscribes and gets a linked dataset
Export the tables to a public Cloud Storage bucket so that customers can download files and load them into their own warehouses each night
Schedule a nightly table copy into a new dataset in every customer's project, which the company owns and pays storage for

stem: A finance dataset has a table with customer names, account numbers and monthly totals. A group of regional analysts needs to query only the monthly totals by region, and must not be able to read the underlying table or dataset. What is the best way to share the data?

choices.text: Create a view that selects only region and monthly totals in a separate dataset, and authorize that view on the source dataset
Copy the table into a new dataset every night with the sensitive columns removed, and grant the analysts access to the copy
Grant the analysts the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the source dataset and ask them not to select the sensitive columns
Give the analysts the BigQuery Job User role in the source project, which allows them to read tables referenced in their queries

stem: A reporting dataset contains 35 views that all read from a central sales dataset. Analysts hold access only to the reporting dataset. New views are added every week, and the team is tired of authorizing each new view on the sales dataset one by one. What should the data engineer configure?

choices.text: Make the sales dataset a public exchange listing so any view can reach it with no further authorization
Grant the analysts the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the sales dataset so that every view works with their credentials
Replace the views with a table copy of each query result and refresh them with scheduled queries
Authorize the reporting dataset on the sales dataset so that all views in it can read the sales data

stem: A data provider shares a licensed dataset through an Analytics Hub listing. An audit shows that a subscriber copied the shared tables into its own project with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT and exports, which breaks the license. The provider wants subscribers to keep querying but not extract the data. What should the provider do?

choices.text: Delete the data exchange and send each subscriber a monthly Cloud Storage export with a signed URL
Make the listing public so that every Google Cloud user can query it, which removes any reason for subscribers to copy the licensed tables
Enable data egress restrictions on the listing so copy, export, snapshot and table writes are unavailable
Ask subscribers to turn off their own project billing so they cannot run extract jobs

stem: Which TWO statements about a linked dataset in Analytics Hub (BigQuery sharing) are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It is a full writable copy of the shared dataset, which the subscriber stores and pays for in its own project
It is a read-only pointer to the shared dataset in the subscriber's project, and creating it does not copy the data
Queries against it are billed to the publisher, because the publisher owns the underlying storage
Subscribers can add or update tables inside it so they can enrich the shared data in place
Subscribers can query it in real time and join it with tables in their own datasets

stem: A supplier shares a pricing dataset through Analytics Hub. The contract limits it to three named retail partners, and the supplier's legal team requires that no other Google Cloud user can even discover it. How should the data engineer set up the sharing?

choices.text: Publish the dataset as a commercial listing on Cloud Marketplace so that the partners can purchase access
Create a public data exchange so that all authenticated users can find it, and rely on the contract for restrictions
Create a public listing in a private exchange so that the three partners can find it without extra IAM grants
Create a private data exchange and a private listing, and grant subscriber access only to the groups of the three partners

stem: A logistics company streams vehicle telemetry into Pub/Sub and wants two partner companies to receive the same events in near real time in their own projects, without the company copying messages or managing partner IAM on its topic. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Write the events to a BigQuery table and give partners the table's dataset editor role to read them
Mirror the topic to a topic in each partner project using a custom Dataflow pipeline running continuously
Share the Pub/Sub topic through an Analytics Hub listing; each partner gets a linked Pub/Sub subscription
Create a push subscription for each partner pointing to a webhook endpoint that the partners must build, secure and keep available

stem: A data platform team of a retailer sets up Analytics Hub in its organization. A data steward must create exchanges and decide who may publish, two engineers must publish listings of their datasets, and 200 analysts must browse and subscribe. Which role assignment follows least privilege?

choices.text: Admin to the steward, Publisher to the two engineers, and Subscriber to the analysts
Analytics Hub Publisher to the steward, Analytics Hub Admin to the analysts, and Subscriber to the engineers
Analytics Hub Viewer to the steward and engineers, and Analytics Hub Subscriber to the analysts
Analytics Hub Admin to everyone involved, since admins can also publish and subscribe in the same exchange

stem: A data team shares an expensive aggregation of billions of web events with 300 internal analysts. The aggregate is refreshed with new events throughout the day. Analysts must query it without any access to the raw events dataset, and the repeated recomputation of the aggregation is driving up cost. What should the team build?

choices.text: A logical view on the raw table, shared by granting analysts the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the raw dataset
A materialized view over the event table, shared as an authorized materialized view in a separate dataset
A dashboard export of the aggregate to a PDF that analysts download from Cloud Storage each morning
A scheduled query that appends the aggregation to a new table every minute, readable by all authenticated users

stem: A publisher shares one large orders table through a single Analytics Hub listing. Several partners subscribe, and each partner must see only the rows for its own sales region. The publisher wants to avoid maintaining a separate table for each partner. What is the best design?

choices.text: Let all partners see every row and ask them to add a region filter to their queries
Apply row-level access policies on the shared table that filter by region for each partner's group
Create a separate dataset and a separate copy of the table per partner, each containing the partner's rows
Encrypt the table with a different customer-managed key per partner so each sees only its own rows

stem: A media company runs a nightly Spark job on a persistent Dataproc cluster that sits idle for about 20 hours a day. All input and output data is in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. The company wants to cut cost without changing the Spark code. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Convert the Spark job into an Apache Airflow PythonOperator that runs in the Cloud Composer environment
Move all input data into HDFS on the cluster, so the job reads local disks and the cluster can be shrunk
Keep the cluster running and buy a larger machine type so the job finishes faster
Run the job from a Dataproc workflow template with a managed cluster that is deleted after the run

stem: Data scientists share a small Dataproc cluster for ad hoc notebooks and queries submitted at unpredictable times by other tools. Clusters were often left running over weekends. What is the simplest control to stop paying for forgotten clusters?

choices.text: Enable autoscaling with a minimum of zero primary workers so the cluster costs nothing while idle
Convert the cluster into a workflow template with a managed cluster, even though jobs are submitted ad hoc
Set scheduled deletion on the cluster with an idle period so it is deleted after a stretch with no running jobs
Ask each scientist to delete the cluster manually each Friday and send a reminder email

stem: A Dataproc cluster for a recurring Spark batch ETL must be cheaper. Input and output are in Cloud Storage and a few failed tasks are tolerable if they are retried. Which TWO actions reduce cost while keeping jobs reliable? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Increase the maximum number of task retries so jobs survive transient task failures from preempted workers
Put all workers on secondary Spot VMs, including the nodes that host HDFS data, to reach the lowest hourly rate
Store the job's intermediate data on secondary workers so that it is removed when they are preempted
Add non-preemptible secondary workers only and size them as large as the primary workers
Add Spot or preemptible secondary workers for extra capacity, keeping them under about half of the total workers

stem: A team enabled autoscaling on a Dataproc cluster with a minimum of two workers so the cluster would "cost almost nothing" overnight. Cost is still high, and the team suspects the policy design. Which guidance from Dataproc best applies?

choices.text: Autoscaling is not meant to shrink idle clusters; delete idle clusters and recreate them, for example with workflows
Raise the autoscaling maximum so that the cluster has more workers to share the idle cost
Combine autoscaling with Spark Structured Streaming so the cluster scales down between micro-batches
Use autoscaling on the on-cluster HDFS utilization metric, which is the best signal for scaling idle clusters

stem: A weekly Dataflow batch pipeline re-indexes product data. It can run any time in a 12-hour window on Sunday, has no GPU needs and does not use Compute Engine reservations. The team wants the lowest compute cost. What should the data engineer enable?

choices.text: Streaming Engine on the batch job, which cuts cost by keeping state of a batch job in a dedicated service
A fixed number of the largest workers with autoscaling off so the job always starts without delay
Flexible Resource Scheduling (FlexRS), mixing preemptible and regular VMs with a scheduling delay
Dataflow Prime vertical autoscaling and a custom worker image, with committed CPU hours on all nodes

stem: One Dataproc cluster runs many short Spark jobs from analysts and also a single eight-hour training-data job. Autoscaling is on, but after a burst of short jobs the cluster stays large for hours, so the bill is high. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Disable graceful decommissioning so that nodes are removed immediately even if a job still uses them
Move the short jobs to the same worker nodes as HDFS, so the large job can borrow their spare memory
Increase the autoscaling cooldown so scale-down decisions are made less often on the shared cluster
Run the eight-hour job on its own cluster and group similar short jobs on another autoscaling cluster

stem: Analysts in a data science project run exploratory queries on BigQuery with on-demand pricing. A few unfiltered queries on very large tables caused an unexpected bill. The data engineer must limit exposure now and help analysts avoid repeats. Which TWO measures should be applied? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Raise the project's slot quota so that queries finish faster and cost less per byte
Have analysts run a dry run, or check the estimated bytes in the query validator, before running a costly query
Move all tables to a spreadsheet tool, which removes the on-demand scan charges for large data
Add LIMIT clauses to every query, which reduces the bytes billed on non-clustered tables
Set custom daily query quotas on the project and per user to cap the data processed per day

stem: A nightly Dataproc workflow often fails at cluster creation in one zone because that zone is short of the requested machine types. Reserved capacity exists in other zones of the same region. The team wants the highest chance that the cluster gets created without hard-coding a zone. What should the data engineer use?

choices.text: Autoscaling on the failed cluster, so the missing machine capacity is added in the same zone later
Auto Zone placement: omit the zone so one is chosen, prioritizing zones with matching reservations
A second cluster in another region that always runs in parallel to take over when the first fails
A cluster pinned to the zone with the lowest price, with a retry loop on creation failures

stem: A data engineer wrote a Cloud Composer DAG whose single task, a PythonOperator, extracts data from an API, cleans it, loads it into BigQuery and sends a notification. When the load step fails, the whole task reruns and the data is duplicated. How should the DAG be redesigned?

choices.text: Split the work into separate idempotent tasks, so a failed step can be retried alone
Raise the task's retry count to the maximum so the same combined task keeps rerunning until it succeeds
Keep one task but add a long sleep before the notification, so the load has time to finish properly
Move the logic into the DAG file's top level, so Airflow runs it every time the scheduler parses the file and the scheduler waits

stem: A Composer DAG fans out one task per customer file, up to 300 tasks at a time, each calling the same partner API. The partner enforces an API quota and has started returning errors during peaks. The team wants to cap simultaneous calls without lowering the DAG's other parallelism. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Reduce the number of Composer scheduler workers for the whole environment to a single worker
Replace the tasks with a SubDagOperator, which serializes all tasks inside it
Split the DAG into 300 DAGs, one per file, each with a distinct schedule time
Assign the API-calling tasks to an Airflow pool with a limited number of slots

stem: A Composer environment runs DAGs that include a task requiring Python libraries that conflict with the environment's installed packages, and another task that needs heavy CPU for an hour. Heavy tasks have slowed the scheduler and other DAGs. What is the recommended design?

choices.text: Use the SubDagOperator to wrap the heavy tasks, as it creates separate resources for them
Install both conflicting libraries into the same environment and accept that DAGs fail on version clashes
Run the isolated tasks with the KubernetesPodOperator against a separate GKE cluster
Run them with the DockerOperator inside the environment, because Composer workers expose a Docker daemon

stem: A genomics lab keeps raw sequencer output in a Cloud Storage bucket. Researchers reopen runs unpredictably, sometimes after months, so the team wants Autoclass to manage storage classes. Enabling it on the bucket fails, because the bucket already has lifecycle rules that move objects to Nearline after 30 days and to Coldline after 90 days, plus a rule that deletes objects after 5 years. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Remove the storage-class transition rules, keep the delete rule, and then enable Autoclass on the bucket
Disable object versioning on the bucket first, because versioning is what blocks Autoclass from accepting lifecycle rules
Move the age-based rules to a second bucket and copy every object there, so Autoclass bucket receives only new uploads
Keep both configurations by raising the bucket's default storage class to Coldline, so Autoclass can start from a colder class

stem: A media-analytics team stores clickstream exports in a Cloud Storage bucket where some days of data are queried again and again and other days are never touched. The team enables Autoclass on the bucket. Which TWO statements describe how Autoclass will manage these objects? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Objects move to colder classes at fixed ages that the owner must list in a lifecycle configuration on the bucket
Every read of an object in a colder class adds a retrieval fee to the bill, as it does with manual Coldline
Objects stay in the class chosen at upload, and Autoclass only reports which objects could be moved
An object that is read is moved back to Standard storage, even if it had already reached a colder class
Objects not accessed for 30 days move to Nearline, which is the default terminal class unless Archive is chosen

stem: A bank must keep payment-audit exports for 7 years. The files are read by dashboards daily during the first 30 days, are opened a few times in the following year for investigations, and after that are almost never read. Access depends only on object age, and the auditors want the transition dates to be exactly predictable. Which storage design fits best?

choices.text: Store every export in Archive storage from the first day, because the data must be kept for such a long period
Enable Autoclass with Standard as the starting class and rely on object reads to decide when each file should move
Upload to Standard, add age-based rules to Nearline after 30 days and Archive after 365 days, and delete at 7 years
Upload to Coldline storage and add a rule that deletes each object after exactly 7 years from its creation

stem: A retail data team exports a weekly snapshot of its product catalog to Cloud Storage. Each snapshot is read about once in the first quarter for reconciliation, then deleted by a lifecycle rule 200 days after creation. The team wants the lowest at-rest cost without paying for time it will not use. Which storage class is the best fit?

choices.text: Archive, because it has the lowest at-rest storage rate of the four standard classes and the data is rarely read
Coldline, because its 90-day minimum storage duration is shorter than the 200 days the data is kept
Nearline, because the snapshots are read a few times and the class has no retrieval fees
Standard, because data that is deleted by a lifecycle rule never qualifies for a colder class

stem: A telecom's BigQuery dataset holds several hundred terabytes of highly repetitive call-detail records. The records compress very well. The dataset uses the default storage billing, the storage bill is the largest line item, and the team wants to lower it with no change to queries, tools or data layout. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Set the physical storage billing model on each table, because the model can only be chosen per table and not per dataset
Export all tables to Cloud Storage as Parquet files and delete the BigQuery tables, so only the compressed files are billed
Compare the logical and physical bytes of the tables, then switch the dataset to the physical storage billing model if it is cheaper
Rewrite every table into a new compressed format, because BigQuery stores data uncompressed by default and bills accordingly

stem: A dataset on physical storage billing holds staging tables that are fully rewritten every night. The storage bill is much higher than the size of the live tables suggests, and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLE_STORAGE shows large time travel byte counts. The team does not need to restore staging data older than two days. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Set the fail-safe period of the dataset to zero, because fail-safe bytes are the part that can be shortened
Set the time travel window on the dataset to the 2-day minimum, which reduces the time travel bytes that are billed
Disable time travel on the dataset, which removes the retained bytes of every rewritten table at once
Switch the dataset back to logical billing, which makes time travel bytes free of charge for every dataset

stem: A clickstream table in BigQuery is partitioned by day on its ingestion time. Compliance allows analysts to see only the most recent 90 days of raw events. The table must stay in place with its schema, and other datasets must not be affected. Which configuration keeps storage from growing without limit?

choices.text: Schedule a weekly query that selects the latest 90 days and overwrites the table with the result
Set a table expiration of 90 days on the table, so that only the oldest partitions are removed first
Set a default table expiration of 90 days on the dataset so older rows are removed from the table
Set a partition expiration of 90 days on the table so each partition is deleted when it is that old

stem: An IoT platform stores billions of per-second sensor readings in BigQuery. Engineers need the detail for the last 60 days, while the business needs only hourly averages and maxima for the following five years. The storage cost of raw rows is growing quickly. What approach keeps long-term metrics while limiting cost?

choices.text: Build a scheduled aggregation into an hourly summary table, then expire the raw partitions after 60 days
Move all raw rows to a Coldline bucket after 60 days and delete the BigQuery table afterwards
Replace the raw table with monthly snapshots that are created on a schedule and kept for five years
Keep all raw rows indefinitely and use clustering on the sensor identifier to reduce the stored bytes

stem: A nightly pipeline rewrites a BigQuery table called ledger_daily. A defect was discovered 12 days after a faulty run changed many rows, and the team could not restore from time travel. Auditors now want an end-of-month copy of the table that can be queried 6 months later, at the lowest storage cost, without a full duplicate of the data. What should the data engineer use going forward?

choices.text: A full copy job each month into a new table, kept until the retention period ends
Table snapshots created at month end, with an expiration of about 6 months
Export each month to Avro files in Archive storage and recreate tables only when requested
Raise the time travel window to 30 days so each month end can be queried from the base table

stem: A ride-sharing company loads trip events into BigQuery from devices that sometimes upload data up to a week late. Analysts always filter by the event timestamp recorded on the device (a TIMESTAMP column named event_ts), usually over a few days. Which partitioning choice gives pruning that matches how the data is queried?

choices.text: Partition by the event_ts column at daily granularity, so late rows still land in the partition of their event date
Partition by an integer range on a derived hour-of-day number, so queries can filter on event time ranges
Leave the table unpartitioned and cluster by event_ts, because clustering gives an exact cost estimate
Partition by ingestion time at daily granularity, because it assigns each row to the partition of its load time

stem: A utility stores 20 billion meter readings in one BigQuery table. Each reading has an integer region_id between 1 and 500, and dashboards nearly always filter on a range of region_id values. No column is a date that the dashboards filter on. Which design reduces the data scanned by these queries?

choices.text: Create one table per region and query them through a wildcard table with a name suffix filter
Cluster the table by a string column that holds the region name, with no partitioning at all
Partition the table by time unit on the load date, so that every region is found in one particular daily partition
Partition by integer range on region_id, with start 1, end 501 and an interval that groups regions

stem: A BigQuery orders table is partitioned by order_date. Reports filter on order_date plus one or more of status and country, and sometimes on status and country alone (without a date range limit). The team wants to cluster the table by status, country and customer_id. Which statement about the clustering column order is accurate?

choices.text: Order does not matter, because BigQuery sorts all clustered columns together and reads blocks
Put the columns in alphabetical order, because BigQuery uses the clustering order as a name index
Order by the filters the queries use, because queries gain most from the leading clustered columns
Put the column with the fewest distinct values last, because high-cardinality columns must be listed first

stem: A team compares partitioning and clustering for a 40 TB BigQuery fact table queried by date and customer. They plan to partition by order date and cluster by customer_id. Which TWO statements about this combination are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: BigQuery automatically maintains the clustering of new data within each partition, using background reclustering
The estimate for a clustered column filter is exact before the run, so no maximum bytes billed setting is needed
Clustering only works on tables that are not partitioned, so the two features cannot be used together
Clustering guarantees that queries need fewer slots, so a smaller reservation will always be enough
A dry run on a query that prunes partitions can show a close estimate of the bytes processed before the query runs

stem: Analysts at a retailer keep running queries on a 15 TB partitioned BigQuery table without a date filter, and each such query scans every partition. Finance wants the platform to stop these queries from running at all, without telling analysts which columns to remember. What should the data engineer configure?

choices.text: Cluster the table by the date column, so that every query is forced to read fewer blocks
Set the Require partition filter option so queries must include a predicate on the partitioning column
Reduce the table's partition expiration to a single day, so that queries cannot reach older partitions in the table at all, and so none can scan them
Enable a materialized view on the table, because it blocks queries that do not use the view

stem: An e-commerce company has three tables for its BigQuery warehouse: orders, order_lines and shipments. Analysts almost always read an order together with its lines, and the lines are never queried without their parent order. Joins between the two tables are slow and costly at their volume. Which redesign does Google recommend for such a parent-child relationship?

choices.text: Move the lines to Bigtable and join them by row key at query time with a federated query
Keep the tables normalized and add a clustering column on the order identifier of the order_lines table
Flatten each order line into a separate row that repeats every order column, creating one wide row per line
Store order lines as a nested and repeated field (an array of structs) inside the order row

stem: A BI team already runs a well-tuned star schema in BigQuery: a sales fact table and six small dimension tables shared by many reports. A new architect proposes folding every dimension into the fact table as flat columns so that joins disappear. What is the best response?

choices.text: Agree, since flattening always improves performance in BigQuery and removes the need to maintain separate dimension tables
Disagree, because BigQuery requires normalized third normal form tables for any query that includes aggregation
Disagree, because a star schema is already an optimized analytics shape and further denormalizing may not change performance much
Agree, because BigQuery cannot run joins efficiently, which is why dimensions have to be folded into the fact table

stem: A weather network loads about 30 MB of observations per day into BigQuery, and the table spans 15 years of history. Backfills frequently touch rows across a wide range of dates. Daily partitions would produce thousands of tiny partitions. Which design is the best fit?

choices.text: Keep daily partitions and add an hourly partition column so each partition holds more rows than before
Avoid partitioning and use only a default table expiration, since small tables are cheaper that way
Use integer-range partitioning on a day number column, with an interval of one, to keep one partition for each separate day
Partition by month on the observation date and cluster on that same date column to sort data within each partition

stem: A data engineer ran an ALTER statement to add clustering on customer_id to a 10 TB BigQuery table that has been loaded for two years. Query bytes for customer lookups on old dates barely changed, while lookups on data loaded after the change scan much less. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Automatic reclustering is billed per query, so the engineer should disable it and cluster manually each night
Clustering takes effect only after a reservation is assigned, so the table needs additional slots for old data
Clustering applies only to newly stored data, so existing rows must be rewritten into the layout
The ALTER statement was rejected silently, so clustering must be recreated by dropping and re-adding the schema

stem: A team on on-demand pricing sets a maximum bytes billed limit on queries against a clustered, unpartitioned 8 TB table. A query that filters on the clustering column is expected to read about 200 GB, but it fails with the error that the query exceeded the limit for bytes billed. Which TWO statements explain the behaviour or suggest a fix? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The limit counts slots, so the team should buy more slot capacity for the project to remove the failure
For clustered tables the pre-run estimate is an upper bound, so the query can fail though the real bytes billed fit
Query results cached from the previous day are counted against the limit and need to be flushed before rerunning it
BI Engine must be turned on for the table, because a limit on bytes billed requires an in-memory cache
Partitioning the table and filtering on the partitioning column gives a more granular estimate before the run

stem: A retailer keeps Parquet files in Cloud Storage and exposes them to BigQuery. The security team needs analysts to query the data with row-level and column-level security, without granting those analysts any permission on the bucket itself. Which table type meets the requirement?

choices.text: A BigLake table with a connection whose service account reads the files, so analysts need only table access
A native BigQuery table loaded from the files, since external data can never carry fine-grained policies
A view over an external table, because a view that selects only some columns hides the data store permissions entirely
A standard external table, because access to the bucket is checked against each analyst's own credentials

stem: A BigLake table points to a Cloud Storage prefix with several million Parquet files laid out by Hive-style partition folders. Queries that filter on the partition folder take minutes just to list objects before reading any data. New files arrive only when a nightly Spark job finishes at a known time. What should the data engineer do?

choices.text: Convert the table to a native table with a nightly insert of every file in the prefix
Enable metadata caching on the table and run a manual refresh of the cache at the end of the nightly job
Replace the BigLake table with a view that unions one table per partition folder
Increase the time travel window of the dataset so that BigQuery keeps its cached object listings for longer

stem: A BigLake table with metadata caching is set to refresh automatically and has a staleness interval of 30 minutes. A data engineer notices that a few queries each day are slower than usual and appear to list files from Cloud Storage. Cache refresh jobs are succeeding. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Automatic refresh takes 30 to 60 minutes, so the cache is sometimes older than the interval and queries read the datastore
The staleness interval is ignored for automatic refresh, so some share of queries always read the datastore at random
Table partitions older than 30 minutes are removed from the cache, causing a lookup of the files
Metadata caching only works for queries that run in the first hour after midnight, so other queries bypass it

stem: A data lake team plans to expose Cloud Storage Parquet data through BigLake tables so that different tools can use it. Which TWO benefits can the team expect? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Data is converted into BigQuery native storage as soon as the table is created, which removes the lake copy
Analysts need Storage Object Viewer on the bucket in addition to table access, so that policies can inspect the files
Spark and other open-source engines that read through the BigQuery Storage API are subject to the same row-level and column-level policies
BigLake tables remove the need for a connection, as users' own identities read the files directly
For Cloud Storage-based tables, dynamic data masking can be applied to hide sensitive column values from selected groups

stem: A lake team keeps an Apache Iceberg table in Cloud Storage and queries it from BigQuery as an Iceberg external table. A colleague suggests enabling metadata caching to speed up planning on this table. What should the data engineer say?

choices.text: Enable it, but only if the table is converted to the CSV format that supports file statistics
Enable it, because Iceberg tables have no metadata and so caching is the only source of file lists
Do not enable it, because metadata caching is available only for native BigQuery tables
Do not enable it, because BigQuery already uses the metadata Iceberg captures in its manifest files

stem: A lake team organizes Parquet files in Cloud Storage for a BigLake table that analysts query mostly by event date and region. At the moment all files sit in one flat folder, and every query opens footers across all of them. Which layout change helps queries prune files?

choices.text: Keep the flat folder and add more columns to each Parquet file for event date and region
Rename every file with a random prefix so objects are spread evenly across Cloud Storage
Write files under Hive-style folders such as dt=2026-11-05/region=eu and define the table with partitioning on them
Compress the whole folder into one archive per month and have the table read each archive as a single large file

stem: A lake keeps raw landing files in a Cloud Storage bucket with soft delete left at its default. A lifecycle rule deletes objects 30 days after creation, but the finance team notices that the bucket's storage charges drop only about a week after the rule runs. What explains this?

choices.text: Lifecycle deletions are queued and run only once per week on a fixed schedule for all buckets
Deleted objects stay soft-deleted for the default retention duration of seven days and can be restored until then
Deleted objects are moved to Archive storage for a week before they are finally removed from the bucket
Object versioning retains a noncurrent copy of every deleted object for the duration of the bucket's life

stem: A lake holds 400 TB of Parquet event data in Cloud Storage exposed through a BigLake table. A small set of 5 TB of the most recent data feeds executive dashboards that run hundreds of times an hour and need consistent low latency. The remaining history is queried a few times a month. Which design best balances cost and performance?

choices.text: Load the recent 5 TB into native BigQuery tables and keep the history in the lake as BigLake tables
Keep everything in BigLake tables, because data in Cloud Storage always queries faster than native storage
Convert the history into one very large CSV file per year, so listing and reading cost the least
Load all 400 TB into native tables and delete the lake copy, so a single storage tier serves every query

stem: A data lake team wants to improve query planning on several BigLake tables. Which TWO tables are good candidates for BigQuery metadata caching? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An Apache Iceberg external table, because its manifest files are slow to read and need caching
A table whose files are overwritten every few seconds and whose queries must always see every change at once
A native BigQuery table partitioned by day, since the cache replaces storage metadata for managed tables
A table over files written by a nightly pipeline at a known time, so the cache can be refreshed manually when the job ends
A table over several million Parquet files in Hive-style folders, where queries filter on the partition folders
